questions.prompt: A cube with edge s is split into three congruent pyramids that share one vertex of the cube as their apex, as shown. Use this, together with scaling and Cavalieri's principle, to explain why EVERY pyramid with base area B and height h has volume ⅓Bh.
questions.prompt_markup: A cube with edge s is split into three congruent pyramids that share one vertex of the cube as their apex, as shown. Use this, together with scaling and Cavalieri's principle, to explain why EVERY pyramid with base area B and height h has volume ⅓Bh.
questions.correct_answer: Each of the three pyramids has volume ⅓s³ = ⅓(s²)(s). Stretching vertically by h/s multiplies the volume by h/s, giving ⅓s²h. Any pyramid with base area B and height h has cross-sections B((h - y)/h)² at height y, the same as a square pyramid with base area B and height h, so by Cavalieri's principle its volume is ⅓Bh.
questions.required_method: (1) Find the volume of one of the three pyramids. (2) Stretch it vertically to any height h. (3) Use Cavalieri's principle to compare any pyramid with a square pyramid of the same base area and height.
questions.grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: (1) the three congruent pyramids fill the cube, each with base s² and height s, so ⅓s³; (2) a vertical stretch extends this to any height; (3) cross-sections are scaled copies of the base with area B((h - y)/h)², so Cavalieri's principle extends it to any base shape and apex position. The cube case alone is NOT sufficient for full credit.

questions.prompt: A triangular prism with base area B and height h is cut into three pyramids (tetrahedra), as Euclid did. Pairs of these pyramids have congruent bases and equal heights. Explain why each pyramid has volume ⅓Bh.
questions.prompt_markup: A triangular prism with base area B and height h is cut into three pyramids (tetrahedra), as Euclid did. Pairs of these pyramids have congruent bases and equal heights. Explain why each pyramid has volume ⅓Bh.
questions.correct_answer: Pyramid 1 and pyramid 2 have equal bases and heights, and so do pyramids 2 and 3, so all three have equal volume. They fill the prism (volume Bh), so each has ⅓Bh; pyramid 1 has the prism's base and height.
questions.required_method: Use the fact that pyramids with equal base areas and equal heights have equal volumes (Cavalieri's principle), applied to two pairs.
questions.grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: two equal-volume pairs give three equal volumes; their sum is Bh; one of them has base B and height h, so V = ⅓Bh.

questions.prompt: In a class experiment, a hollow square pyramid and a hollow square prism have the same base and the same height. It takes three pyramids full of sand to fill the prism. Explain what this shows about the pyramid formula and why it is evidence, not a proof.

questions.correct_answer: The pyramid holds about ⅓ of the prism, Bh, which supports V = ⅓Bh. The experiment has measurement error and tests one pyramid only, so it does not prove the formula for all pyramids.

questions.grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: the ⅓ relationship with the prism; evidence versus proof.

questions.prompt: A cube with edge 6 is split into three congruent pyramids that share one vertex of the cube as their apex. Find the volume of each pyramid, then show that ⅓Bh gives the same value for one pyramid, and explain why this agreement is a check, not a proof for all pyramids.
questions.prompt_markup: A cube with edge 6 is split into three congruent pyramids that share one vertex of the cube as their apex. Find the volume of each pyramid, then show that ⅓Bh gives the same value for one pyramid, and explain why this agreement is a check, not a proof for all pyramids.
questions.correct_answer: Each is 216 ÷ 3 = 72; one pyramid has base 6 × 6 = 36 and height 6, and ⅓ · 36 · 6 = 72. One numerical case cannot cover every pyramid.
questions.required_method: Divide the cube's volume by 3; then compute ⅓Bh for one pyramid.
questions.grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: 216 ÷ 3 = 72; B = 36 and h = 6 for one pyramid; ⅓Bh = 72; a single case is evidence only.

questions.prompt: A square pyramid has base side s and height h. Imagine it built from n stacked square slabs, each of thickness h/n, where the slab k steps from the top has side ks/n. The total slab volume is (s²h/n³) × (the sum of the squares 1², 2², 3², and so on up to n²). For n = 10 and n = 100 this equals 0.385s²h and 0.338s²h. Explain how this supports V = ⅓s²h.
questions.prompt_markup: A square pyramid has base side s and height h. Imagine it built from n stacked square slabs, each of thickness h/n, where the slab k steps from the top has side ks/n. The total slab volume is (s²h/n³) × (the sum of the squares 1², 2², 3², and so on up to n²). For n = 10 and n = 100 this equals 0.385s²h and 0.338s²h. Explain how this supports V = ⅓s²h.
questions.correct_answer: The slabs approach the pyramid as they get thinner, and the coefficients 0.385, 0.338, … approach ⅓, so the volume is ⅓s²h.
questions.required_method: Describe what the slabs approach and what the coefficients approach as n grows.
questions.grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: the slabs approximate the pyramid more closely as n grows; the coefficient trend toward ⅓; conclusion (an informal limit argument).
